title: The Security Deposit Standoff
background: Maya rented a one-bedroom apartment from Evan for 18 months. After moving out, Evan withheld most of her security deposit for cleaning and carpet repairs. Maya demands a full refund; Evan insists the deductions are justified.
facts: Maya moved out on March 1.
Evan withheld $1,200 of the $1,500 security deposit for cleaning and carpet replacement.
Maya left the carpet with three large wine stains and scuff marks on the walls.
Evan had promised in February to replace the aging carpet before Maya's lease ended, but never did.
Maya made a late rent payment in September; Evan sent a written warning about it.
Evan hired a professional cleaning service for $400 after Maya moved out.
Maya gave Evan her new mailing address on March 2.
Evan mailed the itemized deduction list to the old apartment address on April 15, which was 12 days after the legal deadline.
The lease required Maya to return the apartment 'broom-clean and damage-free.'
Maya declined Evan's request for a pre-move-out walkthrough.
dispute: Maya wants the full $1,500 deposit returned, arguing the deductions were untimely, sent to the wrong address, and that Evan had already planned to replace the carpet. Evan wants to keep the $1,200, arguing the unit was left damaged and the cleaning cost was legitimate.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses: late rent payment, left wine stains and scuffs, refused walkthrough, didn't professionally clean; Evan's lapses: missed the itemized-list deadline, sent it to the wrong address, broke his promise to replace the carpet, and the cleaning charge was arguably inflated for the actual work done.

title: The Two-Week Sink Repair and the $50 Communication Fee
background: Maya rents an apartment from David. In early June, her kitchen sink began leaking and the cabinet warped. David arranged a repair that took nearly a month to complete, and afterwards charged Maya a $50 fee for what he called 'extra communication handling.'
facts: On June 1, Maya emailed David: "The kitchen sink is leaking and the cabinet is warping."
On June 3, David replied: "I'll send a plumber next week."
On June 10, no plumber had arrived; Maya sent a second email.
On June 11, David replied: "Plumber is scheduled for June 15."
On June 15, the plumber inspected the sink and said the needed part was not in stock and that he would order it.
On June 20, Maya texted David: "This is getting ridiculous, I expect action this week."
On June 22, David ordered the part online after learning the plumber had not ordered it.
On June 25, Maya sent a formal complaint to the property management company without informing David.
The part arrived on June 28; the plumber fixed the sink on July 1.
On July 2, David sent Maya an invoice for $50 for 'extra communication handling.'
dispute: Maya wants David to waive the $50 fee and apologize for the delay. David wants Maya to pay the $50 and acknowledge that her unilateral complaint to management was unfair.
fault_rationale: David missed his own promised timeline and failed to verify the plumber's order, while Maya sent a snide text and escalated to management without prior notice—each has a concrete lapse.

title: The Lease-Break Fee Dispute
background: Mark rented an apartment to Lisa under a one-year lease, which included an explicit early termination clause.
facts: On January 1, 2025, Mark and Lisa signed a 12-month lease for apartment 4B starting February 1, 2025, with monthly rent of $1200.
The lease states that early termination requires 60 days' notice and payment of a $2000 lease-break fee.
On June 15, 2025, Lisa informed Mark in writing that she would move out on July 1, 2025.
Lisa moved out on July 5, 2025, leaving without paying rent for August.
Mark inspected the apartment and found it undamaged but slightly dusty.
Mark listed the apartment on August 1, 2025, and found a new tenant who moved in on September 1, 2025.
Mark sent Lisa a bill for the $2000 lease-break fee on August 10, 2025.
Lisa responded that she lost her job and had to move to a cheaper city.
Lisa offered to pay $500 as a 'goodwill' fee.
Mark refused the offer and demanded the full $2000 per the lease.
dispute: Mark wants the full $2000 lease-break fee as stated in the lease; Lisa wants to pay only $500 due to financial hardship.
fault_rationale: Lisa clearly violated the lease by moving out early without the required notice and refusing to pay the contractual fee, while Mark followed the lease terms and made reasonable efforts to re-rent the property.

title: The Extended Guest
background: Maya rents an apartment from Tom. Tom lives in the building and manages it himself. Maya’s old college friend, Jake, lost his job and asked to crash for a few weeks. Tom runs a tight ship and monitors lease compliance.
facts: Maya's written lease states any guest staying over 7 days must have prior written landlord approval.
Jake arrived at Maya's apartment on June 1 and slept on her couch.
Maya never requested written approval for Jake, nor did she tell Tom about him until June 10.
On May 20, Maya emailed Tom about a leaking kitchen faucet, and Tom replied he'd fix it by May 25.
Tom did not schedule a plumber until June 12, and only after Maya reminded him again that evening.
On June 10, Tom saw Jake in the hallway and sent Maya a text: 'Get your freeloader out by tomorrow or I'll start eviction proceedings.'
Maya responded on June 11, asking Tom for a one-week extension because Jake was close to finding a job.
Tom refused any extension and demanded Jake leave by June 15, stating it's a matter of lease enforcement.
Jake's presence caused no damage or noise complaints, but Tom noticed extra utility usage and increased wear.
On June 13, Tom sent another email: 'You are in breach. I will not negotiate. Secure your guest's departure.'
dispute: Maya wants Tom to allow Jake to stay until June 30 so Jake can save enough for a deposit. Tom wants Jake gone immediately (by June 15) and Maya to fully comply with the lease's guest clause.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses: she violated the 7-day approval rule and failed to inform Tom about Jake; Tom's lapses: he broke his May 25 promise to fix the faucet and sent two rude, threatening messages instead of a professional notice.

title: The Dog in Apt 2B
background: Maya has rented an apartment from Greg for six months; the dispute is over a small dog Maya brought home without final approval.
facts: On March 1, Maya moved into Greg's apartment.
On May 1, Maya asked Greg for permission to adopt a dog.
Greg said he would reply by May 7 but never did.
On May 15, Maya adopted the dog without Greg's answer.
On May 20, Greg saw the dog and texted Maya, 'I guess you didn't need my permission.'
Maya agreed on May 25 to pay a $200 pet deposit but did not pay it.
On June 10, Greg gave Maya a written notice to remove the dog within 30 days.
On June 20, Greg offered to allow the dog if Maya paid $50 extra per month.
Maya refused the $50 monthly offer on June 22.
On July 5, Maya emailed Greg complaining about the notice and his 'rude tone.'
dispute: Maya wants to keep the dog and only pay the original $200 deposit, which she is now willing to pay. Greg wants the dog removed, or alternatively, the $50 monthly fee.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses are adopting the dog without waiting for Greg's promised reply and failing to pay the agreed deposit; Greg's lapses are breaking his promise to reply by May 7 and sending a rude text on May 20.

title: Utility Bill Dispute
background: Mike rents an apartment from Sarah. The lease stipulates that the tenant must pay utility bills within 10 days of receiving them, and a late fee applies otherwise.
facts: Lease signed on Jan 1, 2022, includes clause that tenant pays utility bills within 10 days of bill receipt.
Water bill for March issued on March 5, amount $45.
Mike received the bill on March 5.
Mike did not pay the bill by March 15.
Sarah sent a reminder email on March 10.
Mike replied on March 12, stating he would pay the following week.
Mike paid the bill on March 20, 15 days after receipt.
Sarah charged a $25 late fee as specified in the lease.
Mike claimed he forgot because he was overwhelmed with work deadlines.
Sarah has never charged a late fee before this instance.
dispute: Mike wants the late fee waived. Sarah wants the late fee paid as per the lease agreement.
fault_rationale: Mike violated the explicit lease agreement by paying 5 days late, while Sarah followed the lease and gave a reminder; Mike's forgetfulness is a weak excuse.

title: Mould in the Bathroom
background: Maya rents an old apartment from Tom, and a persistent mould problem in the bathroom has led to a dispute over who is responsible for the delay and the cost of cleaning.
facts: On March 1, Maya emailed Tom about black mould in the bathroom ceiling.
On March 5, Tom replied that he would send a contractor within two weeks.
On March 12, Maya sent a follow-up email because no contractor had contacted her.
On March 20, Tom's contractor Pete visited and took photos, promising a quote by March 27.
On March 27, Maya emailed Tom asking for the quote.
On April 2, Tom said the quote was too high and he would look for cheaper options.
On March 28, Maya bought a mould removal kit and cleaned the ceiling herself.
On April 5, Maya texted Tom that she would withhold $200 from next month's rent to cover the kit and her time.
On April 5, Tom replied, calling her withholding illegal self-help and demanded the full rent.
On April 10, Maya discovered the mould had spread to the bathroom wall and uploaded photos to the property portal.
dispute: Maya wants Tom to immediately remediate the mould and reimburse her for the cost of the kit and her time; Tom wants Maya to pay the full rent before he will arrange further repairs.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses include cleaning the mould herself and threatening to withhold rent without prior agreement, while Tom's lapses include breaking his promise to send a contractor within two weeks and failing to communicate about the quote in a timely manner.

title: Noise Complaint and Broken Promise
background: Maria rents apartment 2C in a building David owns. She complains about noise from the tenant above her in 2D.
facts: On April 1, Maria signed a one-year lease for apartment 2C.
The lease states tenants must keep noise at a reasonable level after 10 PM.
Starting in May, Maria sent 12 emails to David about loud footsteps from 2D after midnight.
On May 15, David replied that he would talk to the upstairs tenant.
On June 1, Maria played music at her birthday party until 2 AM with windows open.
On June 3, David sent a written warning to Maria about excessive noise.
On June 10, David promised to install carpeting in 2D by July 1 to reduce noise.
On July 10, Maria emailed David that the carpeting was not installed.
On July 12, David responded that the upstairs tenant refused the carpeting, so he would not push further.
On July 15, Maria withheld $200 from the rent, saying it was for the carpeting she had to pay for the noise abatement herself.
dispute: Maria wants David to enforce the lease against the upstairs tenant and to reimburse her for the $200 she withheld for the carpeting she arranged herself. David wants Maria to pay the full rent and to stop complaining, as he claims he has done what he could.
fault_rationale: Maria's lapse was throwing a loud party in violation of the lease, while David's lapses were breaking his promise to install carpeting by July 1 and failing to take further action on her repeated noise complaints.

title: Unpaid Overtime Conflict
background: Maya Chen is a junior graphic designer at Daniel O'Brien's digital marketing agency. During a major client pitch, she worked significant unpaid overtime. Daniel verbally acknowledged her effort but failed to follow through on compensation or policy changes. The conflict escalated when Maya voiced her frustration internally.
facts: In January, Daniel asked Maya to take on extra client work without specifying paid time.
Maya regularly worked 10-12 hour days during the project deadline period.
Daniel verbally promised to 'make it up' with a bonus at the end of the quarter.
Maya submitted a timecard and overtime request on February 15, which Daniel didn't approve.
On March 3, Maya sent a company-wide email complaining about unpaid overtime.
Daniel then sent a private message to Maya stating her hours were excessive and not approved.
Maya missed a scheduled client delivery on March 4 because she took a day off without prior approval.
Daniel said he would adjust the team policy to allow comp time, but never implemented it.
Maya declined to attend an optional Saturday team-building event, citing accumulated unpaid work.
Daniel withheld Maya's annual performance review, leaving her without a raise or feedback.
dispute: Maya wants to be compensated for all unpaid overtime hours and to have her complaint acknowledged without reprisal. Daniel wants Maya to work the required hours without additional pay, to stop airing grievances publicly, and to demonstrate commitment by attending company events.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses include sending a company-wide email (fact 5) and missing a delivery due to an unapproved absence (fact 7); Daniel's lapses include making a verbal promise that was never kept (fact 3) and failing to implement the promised comp time policy (fact 8), as well as withholding the performance review (fact 10).

title: Missed Deadline After Schedule Change
background: Alex and Jordan work in a small marketing department. Jordan changed the deadline for a report two weeks before the original due date, but Alex still missed it.
facts: On September 1, Alex agreed to submit the TPS report by September 30.
On September 15, Jordan emailed all staff that the deadline was moved up to September 25.
On September 15, Alex replied to the email with 'Got it, will adjust.'
On September 20, Jordan reminded Alex that the report was due in five days.
On September 21, Alex said it would be done on time.
On September 25, Alex requested a one-week extension, citing family visiting.
Alex's computer logs show the report file was last opened on September 22.
The report was not submitted on September 25.
On September 26, Jordan sent a formal warning about the missed deadline.
dispute: Alex wants a one-week extension to submit the report. Jordan wants the report submitted immediately without extension and expects Alex to acknowledge the breach of agreement.
fault_rationale: Alex's lapse is breaking the explicit agreement and not starting the work despite the deadline change; Jordan's only action was a reasonable reminder, so no real lapse on Jordan's part.

title: The Post-Launch Raise That Got Lost in the Budget
background: Maya is a senior developer at a small tech startup founded by David. During the Q2 product launch, David verbally promised her a 5% raise as recognition for her extra workload. After the launch, the raise never materialized, leading to a conflict about whether the promise was conditional and how to handle the company's financial constraints.
facts: On April 15, David told Maya she would get a 5% raise after the Q2 product launch.
Maya completed her part of the project but missed the final report deadline by three days.
David sent a company-wide email on July 1 stating all raises were delayed due to budget issues.
Maya had worked extra hours during Q2, and her manager noted her strong performance in a written review.
The company's quarterly financial report showed higher-than-expected revenue for Q2.
David's July email did not specify a new timeline for the raises.
Maya replied to David's email with a sarcastic comment about 'budget magic' and skipped the next team meeting.
David offered Maya an additional week of paid vacation instead of the raise, but she declined.
Maya had previously agreed to take on extra responsibilities in exchange for the raise.
Despite the revenue report, David told Maya that cash flow was tight for the next two months.
dispute: Maya wants the 5% raise now, as promised. David wants Maya to accept the delay and the vacation alternative instead of the raise.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses are missing the report deadline, sending a rude email, skipping a team meeting, and rejecting an offer without discussion; David's lapses are breaking a concrete promise, withholding a raise despite strong performance, delaying without a clear timeline, and using a budget excuse contradicted by actual revenue.

title: Remote Work Flexibility vs. Scheduled Hours
background: Alex works remotely for a small tech company. Jamie is Alex's direct manager. The company recently updated its remote-work policy, but communication and interpretation have led to a conflict.
facts: The updated policy requires employees to work from their home office between 9 AM and 5 PM.
Jamie sent an email on March 2 stating that core hours are now 10 AM to 4 PM, but the email was filtered as spam.
On March 5, Alex worked from a coffee shop during core hours without notifying Jamie.
On March 6, Alex missed a scheduled video call with a client due to internet failure and did not message Jamie until the next day.
On March 7, Jamie changed Alex's schedule to start at 9 AM without discussing it with Alex.
On March 7, Alex sent a message to Jamie saying 'This is unfair' but provided no details.
On March 8, Jamie asked Alex to submit a work plan for the following week; Alex submitted it two days late.
On March 9, Alex worked from a cafe again, citing the March 2 email as permission, but the official policy still said home office.
On March 10, Jamie approved Alex's request for a flexible schedule in writing, then overrode it the next day, citing business needs.
On March 11, Alex sent an email to HR complaining about Jamie's inconsistent enforcement of policy.
dispute: Alex wants to continue working from coffee shops and have the flexible schedule that was originally approved. Jamie wants Alex to adhere strictly to the current official policy (home office, 9-5) and follow the schedule Jamie set.
fault_rationale: Alex's lapses: working from an unapproved location, missing a client call and failing to notify promptly, submitting a plan late, and sending a vague rude message. Jamie's lapses: sending a policy update that was not verified, changing Alex's schedule unilaterally, and overriding a previously approved flexible arrangement without prior discussion.

title: The Late Final Paycheck
background: Maya, a graphic designer, resigns from Dan's design studio with proper notice. Her final paycheck arrives 20 days after the legally required date. Dan admits the delay but blames client non-payment. Maya demands the statutory late penalty; Dan sees no wrongdoing since he eventually paid.
facts: Maya worked as a graphic designer at Dan's studio for two years.
On March 1, Maya gave Dan two weeks' notice of resignation.
Maya worked her final day on March 15.
The employee handbook states final pay is issued on the next regular payday after separation.
The next regular payday was March 31.
On April 1, Maya emailed Dan asking for her final paycheck.
Dan replied on April 2, saying he would pay as soon as his client paid him.
Maya sent a second email on April 10, noting the check was overdue.
Dan did not send the paycheck until April 20.
The paycheck was for the exact amount, but the payment was 20 days late.
dispute: Maya wants Dan to acknowledge the breach and pay the state-mandated late fee for each day the final check was delayed. Dan wants to pay only the base amount already given, arguing he made good on the payment eventually and the client delay was beyond his control.
fault_rationale: Dan violated the explicit written policy on final pay timing and likely state wage laws; Maya's only actions were polite reminders, so the clear fault lies with Dan.

title: The Shift Swap That Fell Apart
background: Jordan works as a cashier in a large retail store. Casey is the shift supervisor responsible for scheduling. Swapping shifts requires manager approval.
facts: On February 10, Jordan agreed to cover a coworker's shift on March 15 because the coworker was going on vacation.
On February 20, Jordan emailed Casey to request swapping that March 15 shift with Alex.
On February 21, Casey replied 'approved' to the swap request.
On February 22, Jordan told Alex that the swap was approved, and Alex scheduled a dental appointment for March 15.
On February 28, Casey posted a schedule that still listed Jordan for March 15 and did not list Alex.
On March 1, Jordan asked Casey via email why the swap was missing; Casey did not respond until March 5, citing 'unexpected staffing needs.'
On March 6, Casey sent a message saying all swap approvals are provisional and that the February 21 approval was an error.
On March 7, Jordan replied to that message with 'This is completely unreasonable.'
On March 10, Casey offered Jordan a different swap for March 22, but Jordan declined because her event was on March 15.
dispute: Jordan wants Casey to honor the original swap so she can attend a family event on March 15. Casey wants to keep Jordan on the shift due to staffing needs and offers a later swap, which Jordan rejects.
fault_rationale: Jordan's lapse is having agreed to cover the March 15 shift before requesting a swap for it; Casey's lapse is approving the swap without checking that commitment, then rescinding approval unilaterally and delaying the response.

title: The Reference Letter That Arrived Late and Read Sour
background: Maria worked under Daniel for two years until she left for a new job. She asked him for a reference letter for her upcoming role. Daniel agreed, but the process became strained, and the final letter was lukewarm.
facts: On June 1, Maria emailed Daniel requesting a reference letter.
On June 2, Daniel replied, agreeing to write the letter and send it by June 10.
On June 12, Maria sent a follow-up email asking about the letter.
On June 15, Daniel responded, saying he needed more time to write it properly.
On June 16, Maria sent a terse email: 'Forget it, I'll find someone else.'
On June 17, Daniel wrote and emailed the letter to Maria's new HR contact.
The letter said Maria was 'competent but often impatient when processes slowed down.'
In May, Maria had sent a similar curt email to a client, and Daniel had warned her about it.
In April, Daniel had promised to give Maria post-project feedback but never did.
dispute: Maria wants Daniel to either rewrite the letter to be more positive or officially withdraw it. Daniel wants to keep the letter as is, asserting it reflects his honest assessment.
fault_rationale: Maria's lapses are the rude June 16 email and the May client email; Daniel's lapses are breaking the April feedback promise and missing the June 10 deadline.

title: The Laptop Access Lockout
background: Alice works as a graphic designer at a small marketing agency. Bob is her direct manager. The dispute centers on Alice's use of her company laptop for personal projects after hours.
facts: The company handbook states that company laptops may only be used for work tasks.
Alice's employment contract does not include a clause about personal laptop use.
Bob sent an all-staff email on May 1 reminding employees that personal projects must not use company equipment.
Alice was on approved leave from April 28 to May 3.
On May 2, Alice used the laptop for five hours to edit a friend's wedding video.
On May 6, Alice used the laptop for two hours to update her personal portfolio website.
Bob reviewed Alice's laptop activity logs on May 8 and noted high data usage on May 2 and May 6.
On May 9, Bob disabled Alice's laptop access and gave her a loaner device.
Alice's client project deadline was May 11; she submitted it on May 13.
On April 15, Alice asked Bob for a new battery; Bob said he would order it by April 20.
dispute: Alice wants her original laptop back and an apology for the unilateral restriction, along with the promised new battery. Bob wants Alice to sign a written acknowledgment that she violated the company policy.
fault_rationale: Alice's lapses: she used the company laptop for personal work on two occasions after the policy reminder and missed her client deadline; Bob's lapses: he broke his promise about the battery and disabled Alice's laptop access without any prior discussion or warning.

title: Shared Dog Custody After Breakup
background: Maya and James adopted Max together during their relationship and separated in June. They share no other assets, but both love Max and want primary custody.
facts: On March 12, Maya and James adopted a 2-year-old rescue dog named Max.
In June, they broke up; Maya moved out but Max stayed with James in the apartment.
James agreed that Maya could take Max on weekends if she gave 48 hours notice.
On July 4, Maya showed up unannounced to take Max for the weekend, but James had already left town.
On July 22, James missed a scheduled weekend handoff because he had to work, and didn't tell Maya until the evening before.
On August 5, Maya sent James a series of angry text messages calling him irresponsible.
In August, Maya rented a dog-friendly apartment and asked for a formal 50/50 schedule; James refused.
On September 2, James took Max to the vet for a routine checkup without telling Maya, though she had been the one to book the appointment originally.
On September 15, Maya cancelled her weekend visit at the last minute because she had a party, and James had already planned a hiking trip with Max.
On September 20, James told Maya she could only see Max twice a month, and that he was considering moving to another city.
dispute: What Maya wants now: equal 50/50 custody with a fixed schedule. What James wants now: to keep primary custody and give Maya limited visitation (two weekends a month) and to have final say on care decisions.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses: unannounced visit, angry texts, last-minute cancellation. James's lapses: missed handoff without prompt notice, unilateral vet decision, imposing a reduced schedule and moving threat without discussion.

title: Couch Split After Breakup
background: Emma and Liam were together for three years and lived together for two. They bought a sectional couch during that time. After their breakup, they must decide what to do with it.
facts: Emma and Liam bought a sectional couch for $1000 on March 15.
Emma chose the couch and placed the order without showing Liam other options.
Liam agreed to pay $500 but transferred only $400 on April 5.
Emma covered the remaining $600 from her savings.
Liam missed the pickup date on October 1, so Emma paid a $50 delivery fee to her new apartment.
Emma allowed Liam to use the couch for the first month after the breakup.
Liam left a rude voicemail on October 10 demanding the couch.
Emma posted a photo of the couch on social media on October 12 with the caption 'my couch'.
Liam offered Emma $300 to keep the couch.
Emma proposed selling the couch and splitting the proceeds equally.
dispute: Emma wants to sell the couch and split the proceeds 50/50. Liam wants to keep the couch and pay Emma $300.
fault_rationale: Emma made unilateral decisions about the purchase and publicly claimed ownership, while Liam failed to pay the full agreed amount, missed the pickup deadline, left a rude voicemail, and undervalued the couch in his offer.

title: Sold the Concert Ticket
background: Lena and Mark bought two tickets for a concert while dating. They broke up two months later but agreed to still attend together as friends.
facts: On March 3, Lena and Mark bought two concert tickets for $120 each.
They agreed to attend the June 10 concert together.
On May 10, Mark canceled his work trip.
On May 20, Mark confirmed his attendance and asked about dinner plans.
On May 25, Lena sold her ticket to a coworker for $100.
Lena did not tell Mark about the sale until June 5.
On June 5, Lena told Mark she had sold her ticket.
On June 6, Mark said he was upset and wanted to go.
Lena said she thought Mark would not want to go because of his work trip.
A new ticket for the concert costs $240.
dispute: Lena wants to give Mark the $100 she received and skip the concert. Mark wants Lena to buy a new ticket for $240 so they can both attend as promised.
fault_rationale: Lena broke the explicit agreement to attend together by selling her ticket without telling Mark, while Mark did nothing wrong; her excuse is weak because Mark had already canceled his trip and confirmed his attendance.

title: Returning Belongings After a Messy Breakup
background: Alex and Jamie broke up after a few years together. Alex left some personal items at Jamie's apartment. Both are now in a dispute about how the items should be returned and who is responsible for the extra shipping costs.
facts: On May 1, Alex and Jamie ended their relationship.
Alex left personal belongings at Jamie's apartment.
On May 5, Alex texted Jamie: "I'll pick up my stuff on Saturday."
On May 6, Alex did not show up or message.
On May 8, Jamie texted Alex: "Can you pick up your stuff this week? I'm moving out on June 1."
On May 9, Alex replied: "I can't, I'm away for work until June 15."
On May 20, Jamie shipped Alex's items to an old address that Alex had updated a year ago.
On June 2, the package was returned to sender because the tenant at the old address had moved out.
On June 3, Alex demanded that Jamie cover the shipping cost and apologise.
dispute: Alex wants Jamie to ship the items to his current address at Jamie's expense and to apologise for sending them to the wrong place. Jamie wants Alex to take responsibility for the mix-up and pay the new shipping cost, since Alex had ample time to arrange a pickup.
fault_rationale: Alex's lapse was breaking his promise to pick up on Saturday without notifying, and Jamie's lapse was mailing items to an outdated address without confirming the current one.

title: Unpaid Streaming Bill After Breakup

party_a.name: Alex
party_a.role: ex-partner who paid the annual subscription

party_b.name: Jamie
party_b.role: ex-partner who agreed to reimburse monthly share

background: Alex and Jamie, who used to live together, kept a shared streaming account after their breakup.
facts: In September, Alex paid $120 for a 12-month streaming subscription.
In October, Alex and Jamie agreed to split the monthly cost.
On January 1, they decided to end their relationship and live apart.
On January 2, they agreed Jamie would keep using the account and pay Alex $10 per month for the remaining 6 months.
From January to July, Jamie used the streaming service every month.
By July 31, Jamie had made no payments for these six months.
On July 15, Alex sent Jamie a text reminding him about the $60 owed.
On July 16, Jamie replied, "I thought that was my birthday present."
Alex has not changed the password or restricted Jamie's access at any time.
Jamie's bank statement shows regular purchases at restaurants and movie theaters during the same period.
dispute: Alex wants Jamie to pay the $60 owed for the streaming subscription. Jamie wants to avoid payment, claiming the subscription was a birthday gift.
fault_rationale: Jamie clearly violated the explicit January 2 agreement to reimburse Alex, and his weak excuse is contradicted by the documented arrangement and his continued use of the service.

title: The Unpaid Loan and the Unauthorized Collection
background: Alex and Jordan dated for two years, lived together, and broke up in early 2023. After the breakup, Alex lent Jordan money to cover moving costs.
facts: In March 2023, Alex lent Jordan $2,000 to cover moving costs.
The loan was agreed verbally with a repayment deadline of December 31, 2023.
Jordan repaid $200 monthly from April to June 2023, totaling $600.
In July 2023, Jordan stopped repaying, saying a bank transfer would cover the remainder by Christmas.
In September 2023, Alex took $300 from Jordan's wallet as partial repayment.
In October 2023, Alex sold Jordan's old bicycle for $150, keeping the proceeds.
On December 20, 2023, Jordan sent a message promising the full amount by January 15, 2024.
On January 15, 2024, Jordan did not pay, telling Alex that the debt was void because of Alex's theft.
In February 2024, Alex demanded the remaining $1,400, but Jordan claimed the $450 taken already covered the rest.
dispute: Alex wants Jordan to repay the remaining $1,400. Jordan insists that Alex's unauthorized taking of $300 and the bicycle sale have settled the debt, so he owes nothing.
fault_rationale: Jordan's lapses are missing the December deadline, stopping payments early, and breaking his promise to pay by Christmas; Alex's lapses are taking $300 from Jordan's wallet and selling Jordan's bicycle without permission.

title: The Wedding Plus-One
background: Maya and Ethan broke up three months ago after a three-year relationship. They share many friends and are both invited to the same wedding. The bride asked Maya to help with seating, creating conflict.
facts: Maya and Ethan dated for three years and broke up in March.
The wedding invitation was addressed to both of them.
Maya RSVPed for both without asking Ethan.
Ethan texted Maya that he would bring his new girlfriend.
Maya replied that's disrespectful and blocked his number.
The bride asked Maya to coordinate the seating chart.
Maya placed Ethan at a table with people he barely knew.
Ethan contacted the bride to demand a different seat.
The bride told Ethan about Maya's panic attack at a recent party.
Ethan changed his RSVP from yes to no and back to yes.
dispute: Maya wants Ethan to not bring his new girlfriend and to sit at the table she planned. Ethan wants Maya to stop controlling the wedding arrangements and accept that he can bring a guest.
fault_rationale: Maya unilaterally RSVPed and moved Ethan's seat without consulting him, while Ethan announced his plus-one and changed his RSVP without informing Maya.

title: The Cancelled Cabin Trip

party_b.name: Daniel
party_b.role: ex-partner who had a work conflict

background: Maya and Daniel dated for two years and broke up three months ago. They remained on friendly terms and kept a previously planned weekend cabin trip, splitting the cost.
facts: On March 1, Maya and Daniel agreed to split the cost of a weekend cabin trip in April.
On March 3, Maya paid the full $400 deposit to the cabin owner; Daniel promised to reimburse his $200 half by April 1.
On March 20, Daniel learned of a mandatory work training on the trip weekend, but didn't tell Maya.
On March 28, Maya saw Daniel's public post about attending a music festival that same weekend.
On March 30, Maya texted Daniel, "You're selfish," and then cancelled the cabin reservation herself.
The cabin owner kept $300 of the $400 deposit as a cancellation fee, refunding only $100.
On April 2, Daniel transferred $200 to Maya, writing "for my half, but I never agreed to cancel."
On April 5, Daniel asked Maya to return his $200 since she cancelled without his consent.
Maya refused, saying the $300 loss is Daniel's fault for hiding his plans, and she already spent the $100 refund on a new non-refundable train ticket.
dispute: Maya wants to keep Daniel's $200 to cover the $300 she lost, arguing he owes his share for a trip he abandoned. Daniel wants his $200 back, arguing Maya's unilateral cancellation voided his obligation.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses are the unilateral cancellation of the reservation and the rude message; Daniel's lapses are failing to disclose his work conflict before the payment deadline and making the payment two days late.

title: The Overhanging Maple: A Trimming Dispute

party_a.name: Mark
party_a.role: homeowner who owns the large maple tree

party_b.name: Susan
party_b.role: next-door neighbor whose yard the tree overhangs

background: Mark's maple tree has grown large branches over Susan's yard, dropping leaves and blocking her garden's sunlight for two years.
facts: On April 15, Mark verbally promised Susan that he would trim the branches overhanging her yard by June 1.
On May 28, Susan sent Mark a text reminding him of the June 1 deadline.
On June 1, Mark did not trim the branches and did not reply to Susan's text.
On June 3, Susan hired a licensed arborist to trim the branches back to the property line.
On June 3, the arborist cut a branch that was 3 feet over the fence line.
On June 3, the arborist also cut a branch that was 1 foot on Mark's side of the fence.
On June 4, Mark inspected the tree and found the 1-foot cut branch was already split, but the arborist did not consult him before cutting.
On June 5, Mark sent Susan a bill for $400 to remove the now-unbalanced split branch.
On June 8, Susan offered to pay $100, stating she only authorized the overhang removal.
On June 10, Mark left a voicemail calling Susan a trespasser and refused any compromise, demanding the full $400.
dispute: Mark wants Susan to pay the full $400 for the damage to his side of the tree. Susan wants to pay only $100, arguing Mark's broken promise and silence forced her to act unilaterally.
fault_rationale: Mark's lapses are breaking his promise and ignoring Susan's reminder; Susan's lapses are unilaterally hiring the arborist without a final warning, and the arborist cutting over the property line.

title: The Shared Fence Repair Dispute
background: Maya and Tom are next-door neighbors sharing a wooden fence. After a storm broke a section, they agreed to repair it, but disagreements over costs and communication spiraled.
facts: On March 5, a storm broke a 6-foot section of the fence between Maya's and Tom's yards.
On March 8, Maya and Tom agreed to split the cost of repairing the fence and that Maya would get three quotes.
By March 20, Maya had not provided any quotes, so Tom contacted a contractor himself.
On March 22, Tom hired the contractor without telling Maya beforehand.
On March 25, Tom left a voice message for Maya calling her 'unreliable' for not following through.
On March 28, the contractor repaired the fence section, but also trimmed one of Maya's rose bushes, damaging it.
On April 2, Tom sent Maya a bill for her half ($600) and a photo of the completed fence.
On April 10, Maya told Tom she would not pay until he paid for her damaged rose bush, which she valued at $250.
On April 15, Tom wrote a check for the rose bush but stated he felt it was not his responsibility.
On April 20, Maya still had not paid the $600, saying she wanted to inspect the work first.
dispute: Maya wants to deduct the $250 cost of her damaged rose bush from the $600 fence payment and wants an apology for Tom's rude message. Tom wants Maya to pay the full $600 without deductions, arguing he already paid for the rose bush separately, and wants an apology for her delay.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapse was breaking her promise to provide quotes on time and delaying payment; Tom's lapse was making a unilateral decision to hire the contractor and sending a rude message, with his contractor causing property damage.

title: The Barking Dog and the Loud Music
background: Maria lives in a small house with her dog, a rescue beagle named Max. John lives next door and works from home. They have been neighbors for three years, with no prior conflicts until this spring.
facts: Max barks for 10–15 minutes each weekday morning when Maria leaves for work at 8:00 a.m.
On June 5, John wrote a note to Maria asking her to keep Max quiet during his work hours.
Maria texted John the same day, saying she would order a bark collar by June 10.
Maria did not place the order because her mother was hospitalized on June 8.
On June 12, John called the non-emergency police line about the barking; the police spoke to Maria and left without a citation.
On June 15, John began playing loud hip-hop music in his backyard from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. to mask the dog's barking.
A third neighbor, Sam, asked John twice to lower the music, saying it was vibrating their shared fence.
On June 20, John emailed Maria a detailed log of 14 barking episodes over the previous two weeks, with dates and durations.
Maria responded by email, apologizing but explaining that John's music had added stress and she feared retaliation.
On June 25, John declined a mediator's offer, stating he wanted Maria to 'actually do something' instead of talking.
dispute: Maria wants John to stop the loud music and give her one more month to train her dog with the bark collar she has now purchased. John wants Maria to permanently keep Max from barking during the day and to reimburse him for the cost of sound-blocking headphones he bought.
fault_rationale: Maria's lapse is breaking her promise to order the bark collar by June 10; John's lapse is unilaterally playing loud music despite neighbor complaints, plus his escalated email tone and refusal to mediate.

title: The Parking Spot Promise
background: Emily and Raj are next-door neighbors in a quiet street. Emily's house lacks a driveway, so she relies on street parking. Raj has a two-car driveway and an extra car that he sometimes parks on the street.
facts: Emily's house has no driveway, so she parks on the street.
Raj's house has a two-car driveway, and he owns two cars.
Raj often parks one of his cars in the street spot directly in front of his house.
In April, Raj told Emily he would keep that spot empty for visitors, not park his own car there.
On May 3, Raj parked his own car in that spot and left it for five days.
On May 5, Emily texted Raj asking him to move the car because her parents were visiting.
Raj did not reply to the text and did not move the car until May 8.
On May 10, Emily parked her car in that spot and left it for ten days, ignoring Raj's request to move it for a furniture delivery on May 14.
On May 20, Raj put up a hand-painted sign saying 'Reserved for Raj' without asking the city.
On May 21, Emily left a sarcastic note on Raj's windshield: 'Great parking etiquette'.
dispute: Emily wants to use the street spot whenever she needs it, without Raj reserving it for himself. Raj wants to keep the spot exclusively for his own vehicles and guests.
fault_rationale: Emily ignored Raj's specific request to move her car for a delivery and left it for ten days; Raj broke his promise not to park his own car in the spot and unilaterally claimed it with a sign.

title: The Late-Night Party
background: Maya and Tom live next door to each other in a quiet suburb. On Friday, Maya threw a birthday party in her backyard.
facts: On Friday, Maya sent a group text to neighbors saying the party would run from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.
At 11 p.m., music from Maya's backyard was audible on Tom's property.
Tom texted Maya at 11:30 p.m. with the message: 'TURN IT DOWN NOW. You knew the rules.'
Maya replied at 11:45 p.m., saying she would turn the music down.
The music stopped at 12:05 a.m.
Tom used a phone app to record sound levels from his backyard at 10:30 p.m., 11:00 p.m., and 11:30 p.m.
At 9:30 p.m., Maya had reminded all guests to keep noise low and leave quietly after 10 p.m.
Tom's security camera recorded a guest urinating on his fence at 12:15 a.m.
Maya offered Tom $100 to pay for a pressure wash of the fence.
Tom's wife told him he was overreacting about a one-time party.
dispute: Maya wants Tom to accept her fence-cleaning offer and stop sending hostile messages. Tom wants Maya to sign a written agreement that all future parties end by 10 p.m. and to formally apologize to him and the neighborhood association.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapse is breaking her own stated 10 p.m. end time, and Tom's lapse is sending a rude, all-caps message rather than a polite request.

title: Security Camera Angle
background: Marcus and Elena live next door. On March 2, Marcus agreed in writing that his new security camera would cover only his own side yard. Elena noticed the camera also showed her side yard and window, and asked Marcus to fix it.
facts: On March 2, Marcus signed a short agreement stating his camera would cover only his side yard.
Marcus installed the security camera on March 5.
On March 7, Elena saw the camera's live view on Marcus's phone and noticed her side yard and window were visible.
Marcus said he adjusted the angle to cover a blind spot near his back door.
Elena showed Marcus the signed agreement on March 8.
Marcus said the agreement was about the porch camera, not the yard camera.
The camera's field of view included Elena's side window and part of her driveway.
Elena asked Marcus on March 8 to re-aim the camera to match the agreement.
On March 12, Elena checked and the camera angle had not changed.
Elena left a note on Marcus's door on March 12 asking him to respond.
Marcus said the camera was for his family's safety and moving it would leave a blind spot.
dispute: Marcus wants to keep the current camera angle to avoid a blind spot. Elena wants Marcus to re-aim the camera to comply with the signed agreement.
fault_rationale: Marcus's lapse is signing an explicit agreement limiting the camera to his own property, then aiming it to include Elena's yard and window and ignoring her request; Elena's only action was asking him to comply with the agreement, which is reasonable.

title: The Wet Bookshelf
background: Alice's parcel was delivered to Bob's house while she was away, and Bob took it inside. After a week of no response from Alice, Bob moved it to his porch where it was damaged by rain. They disagree about who is responsible for the damage.
facts: On June 1, a courier left a cardboard box for Alice at Bob's front door because she wasn't home.
Bob found the box on his doorstep that evening and brought it inside to keep it dry.
On June 2, Bob texted Alice: 'I have your package. Come get it by Friday.'
Alice was on vacation until June 10 and did not reply to Bob's message.
On June 12, Bob placed the box on his back porch because he needed the space.
On June 15, heavy rain soaked the box; the bookshelf inside warped.
On June 10, Alice returned and, not finding the package, filed a complaint with the courier.
The courier told Alice on June 13 that Bob had accepted the package.
Bob had told Alice in May that he would only hold packages for one week.
Alice had asked Bob in May to accept packages for her whenever he was home, and Bob had agreed.
dispute: Alice wants Bob to reimburse the cost of the damaged bookshelf because he took responsibility for the package and let it get ruined. Bob wants Alice to stop blaming him because she ignored his deadline and extended holding time without communication.
fault_rationale: Alice's lapses: she didn't reply to Bob's message about the package, missing his stated one-week deadline; Bob's lapses: he moved the package outdoors violating his implied care, after initially agreeing to accept packages, and he didn't follow up or protect it properly.

title: Snow Clearing on the Shared Path
background: Margaret and Tom live next door and share a path that connects both front doors to the street. They have an informal agreement to alternate clearing snow after each storm.
facts: On December 1, Margaret and Tom agreed to alternate clearing snow from the shared path.
Each neighbor’s responsibility started after each snowfall.
A snowstorm dropped 8 inches on the evening of December 10.
Margaret cleared the path on the morning of December 11.
A second storm deposited 5 inches on the evening of December 15.
Under the agreement, Tom was responsible for clearing after the December 15 storm.
Tom did not clear the path on December 16 or 17.
On December 18, Margaret slipped on the path while walking to her car; she was not injured.
On December 18, Margaret texted Tom, and Tom replied, "I've worked double shifts all week—you take this one."
dispute: Margaret wants Tom to clear the snow immediately and honor the agreement going forward. Tom wants Margaret to clear it this time because he is exhausted, suggesting he will do it next time.
fault_rationale: Tom broke the explicit agreement and left a known hazard, while Margaret followed the agreement and only reminded him after a fall; her only possible lapse is not reminding earlier, but that is not a real fault.

title: Dishes, a Mug, and a Missing Rule
background: Maya and Jordan have shared a two-bedroom apartment for six months. They have a written roommate agreement about kitchen chores and quiet hours.
facts: On Monday, Maya did not wash her breakfast dishes before leaving for class.
On Tuesday, Jordan hosted two friends for a study dinner, using four extra plates and two bowls.
On Tuesday night, Jordan left the used dishes in the sink and went to bed.
On Wednesday morning, Maya sent Jordan a text: 'Can you please handle your mess?'
On Wednesday afternoon, Jordan replied: 'I'm not your maid, I had a work deadline.'
On Wednesday evening, Maya threw away a chipped ceramic mug that Jordan had kept on the shelf.
On Thursday, Maya washed all the dishes in the sink, including Jordan's extras.
On Friday, Jordan washed the remaining dishes and placed them in the drying rack.
The roommate agreement from September states: 'Each person washes their own dishes within 24 hours of use.'
On Thursday evening, Maya told Jordan that the mug was in the way and it's gone.
dispute: Maya wants Jordan to follow the 24-hour dish rule strictly and to acknowledge that Maya cleaned up Jordan's mess. Jordan wants Maya to apologize for throwing away the mug without asking and to stop sending rude texts, since Jordan also cleans up.
fault_rationale: Maya's lapses are skipping her Monday dishes, sending a rude text, and unilaterally disposing of Jordan's mug; Jordan's lapses are leaving dishes overnight in violation of the 24-hour rule and responding defensively instead of apologizing.

title: The Guest Who Overstayed
background: Sarah and Emily share a two-bedroom apartment with a written roommate agreement that each partner may stay over a maximum of two nights per week.
facts: The signed roommate agreement states 'each partner stays over max 2 nights per week'.
On Monday, March 3, Emily's partner Jake arrived at the apartment at 7 PM.
Jake stayed over Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday nights that week.
Sarah texted Emily on Thursday morning: 'Jake has been here 3 nights, remember the 2-night rule?'
Emily replied: 'I know, but he's had a rough week, just this once.'
On Friday, March 7, Sarah found Jake's toothbrush and phone charger in the bathroom.
Sarah counted five nights total for the week in her calendar app.
Emily paid her share of utilities on time and never complained about Sarah's guests.
Sarah had not invited anyone over in the past month.
On Saturday, March 8, Sarah asked Emily to ask Jake to leave for the weekend; Emily said he was already gone.
dispute: Sarah wants Emily to adhere strictly to the two-night limit going forward and to confirm in writing that Jake won't exceed it again. Emily wants flexibility for occasional longer visits, citing Jake's stressful period.
fault_rationale: Emily's lapse is clear: she violated the explicit written agreement (five nights vs. two), while Sarah's only action was enforcing the rule politely, with no comparable breach.

title: The Unilateral Upgrade and the Late Payment
background: Alex and Sam share a two-bedroom apartment and split utility bills. Their dispute is over who owes what for the internet after a plan change and a late payment.
facts: On February 1st, Alex and Sam agreed to split the internet bill equally, paying by the 5th of each month.
On March 15th, Alex changed the internet plan from 100 Mbps to 500 Mbps, increasing the monthly cost from $60 to $80.
Alex did not mention the plan change to Sam until April 1st, when the $80 bill arrived.
Sam was away from the apartment for 12 days in March visiting family.
On April 5th, Sam paid $30 to Alex for the March internet bill.
On April 6th, Alex sent Sam a message saying, "You owe the full $40 for April. Pay up or get your own router."
Alex works from home full-time and uses a VPN for work, which requires a stable connection. Sam uses the wifi for gaming and streaming social media.
On March 10th, Sam had told Alex they would handle the payment coordination for March, but forgot to send the money until April 5th.
The previous plan (100 Mbps) was sufficient for both of their uses, according to an online speed test they both ran in February.
On April 10th, Sam told Alex they would only pay $10 more for the upgrade, since they were not consulted and were away for part of the month.
dispute: Alex wants Sam to pay the full $40 share for April and the $40 share for March, including the upgrade cost. Sam wants to pay only the original $30 for each month, refusing the upgrade cost because they were not consulted and were absent for part of the billing period.
fault_rationale: Alex's lapses are the unilateral plan change on March 15th and the rude message on April 6th; Sam's lapses are failing to coordinate the March payment as promised on March 10th and paying the March bill late on April 5th instead of the agreed-upon date.

title: The Broken TV and the Emergency Fund
background: Jordan and Sam share an apartment and bought a TV together a year ago. The TV recently broke, and they disagree on how to replace it.
facts: On March 1, Sam dropped the TV remote, cracking the screen.
On March 2, Jordan promised to fix the unstable shelf but didn't do it.
On March 5, Jordan offered to split the repair cost, but Sam declined, saying it was an accident.
On March 10, Sam bought a new TV for $500 using their shared emergency fund without telling Jordan.
On March 12, Jordan sent Sam a rude message calling the purchase 'selfish'.
On March 15, Sam said the old TV was beyond repair and a new one was necessary.
Jordan had been saving the emergency fund for a planned trip in April.
Both agreed on March 1 to split any repair costs, but Sam made a unilateral decision later.
The new TV costs $500, which is exactly what Jordan had saved for the trip.
dispute: Jordan wants Sam to return the new TV and split the cost of repairing the old one. Sam wants to keep the new TV and have Jordan contribute half of its cost.
fault_rationale: Jordan's lapses are the broken promise to fix the shelf and the rude message, while Sam's lapses are ignoring the earlier agreement and unilaterally spending shared emergency funds on a new TV without consent.

title: The Shared Fridge: A Tale of Leftovers and Promises
background: Alex and Jordan are roommates in a shared apartment with one fridge.
facts: On January 1, Alex and Jordan agreed that Alex would cook dinner, and Jordan would pay $50 weekly for groceries.
On January 8, Jordan paid $30 and said she would pay the remaining $20 on January 15.
On January 12, Alex ate the remainder of Jordan's Thai food from the fridge.
On January 13, Jordan texted Alex that taking the Thai food without asking was rude.
On January 14, Alex replied he would replace the Thai food.
On January 14, Alex prepared a large lasagna and placed it in the fridge.
On January 15, Jordan took the lasagna and ate it for lunch.
On January 15, Alex was away at work the whole day.
On January 16, Alex saw the empty lasagna container in the trash.
On January 16, Jordan told Alex she considered the lasagna to be shared because of the cooking agreement, and reminded him of the unpaid $20.
dispute: what A wants now: Alex wants Jordan to replace the lasagna or pay for it, since it was his personal meal for the week; what B wants now: Jordan wants Alex to pay the $20 she is owed, and to acknowledge that the lasagna fell under their food-sharing agreement.
fault_rationale: Alex's lapses: he ate Jordan's Thai food without asking, failed to replace it, and accepted a partial grocery payment without clarification; Jordan's lapses: she did not pay the full $50 on time, and took the lasagna without confirming it was meant to be shared.

title: The Thermostat Standoff
background: Alex and Bailey share a two-bedroom apartment. The hallway thermostat controls the whole unit. They have been roommates for eight months and generally get along, but temperature preferences have caused friction.
facts: On October 1, Alex set the thermostat to 72°F without telling Bailey.
On October 2, Bailey changed it to 68°F and left a sticky note that read 'keep it reasonable.'
In the first week of October, Alex and Bailey agreed to a schedule: 72°F from 6-9am and 6-11pm, 68°F otherwise.
On October 3, Bailey hosted friends until 2am; the thermostat stayed at 68°F all night, despite the agreement.
On October 4, Alex turned the thermostat up to 74°F during the day because he had a cold, but did not mention it to Bailey.
On October 5, Bailey lowered the thermostat to 65°F while Alex was at work, assuming Alex wouldn't notice.
On October 6, Alex texted Bailey: 'Stop messing with the thermostat without asking.'
On October 7, Bailey replied: 'You do the same thing. I'm not a mind reader either.'
On October 8, both adjusted the thermostat three times in one day, each without consulting the other.
On October 9, they agreed to discuss the issue, but neither apologized for their earlier actions.
dispute: Alex wants a fixed schedule with 72°F during his requested hours, and for Bailey to respect it. Bailey wants more flexibility and a default of 68°F, with no unilateral changes by either.
fault_rationale: Alex broke the agreed schedule, made unilateral changes (including setting 74°F), and failed to communicate his cold; Bailey also broke the schedule, made unilateral changes (including 65°F), and sent a blunt sticky note and text reply.

title: Moving Out Early: Broken Lease
background: Casey and Jordan are roommates sharing a two-bedroom apartment under a one-year lease. Casey decides to move out four months early for a new job, leaving Jordan to cover the full rent.
facts: On September 1, Casey and Jordan signed a 12-month lease, from October 1 to September 30.
The lease requires equal sharing of rent and utilities.
On March 15, Casey informed Jordan of an intention to move out at the end of April.
Casey received a job offer requiring relocation by May 1.
On April 20, Casey moved out and took all personal belongings.
Casey paid rent for April but not for May through September.
On April 25, Jordan emailed Casey demanding the remaining rent.
Casey responded that they could not afford to pay for months they would not live in the apartment.
On April 28, Jordan posted an ad for a new roommate on a rental website.
No replacement was found before the lease ended on September 30.
dispute: Casey wants to be released from the lease and not pay rent for months after moving out. Jordan wants Casey to honor the lease and pay their share of rent until the lease ends or a new roommate is found.
fault_rationale: Casey violated the explicit written lease agreement by moving out early and refusing to pay the remaining months, while Jordan honored the lease and made reasonable efforts to find a replacement.

title: The Noisy Work-From-Home Schedule

party_a.name: Jordan
party_a.role: customer support specialist working from home

background: Jordan and Taylor share a two-bedroom apartment. Jordan's job requires taking client calls, often at irregular hours due to time zones. Taylor's coursework demands quiet periods for studying and group projects. They made a schedule to balance noise and quiet, but recent events have strained the arrangement.
facts: On March 1, Jordan and Taylor agreed that Jordan would only take calls between 2–5 PM, and Taylor would keep common areas quiet during those hours.
Jordan took a call from a client at 8:15 AM on April 3 due to a last-minute deadline issue.
Jordan did not notify Taylor before taking the early-morning call.
Taylor invited two classmates to work on a group project in the living room from 2:30–4:45 PM on April 5.
Taylor informed Jordan about the study group one day in advance.
Jordan moved his desk to the bedroom for the rest of the week because the living room was too noisy during the study group.
On April 6, Taylor texted Jordan: 'You broke our agreement by calling at 8 AM. Please stick to 2–5 PM.'
Jordan replied: 'That was an emergency, but you also broke it by having people over during my call hours.'
The apartment has separate bedrooms, but the living room is shared and the walls are thin.
dispute: Jordan wants Taylor to tolerate occasional early-morning calls as part of Jordan's job and to stick to the agreed quiet hours during 2–5 PM. Taylor wants Jordan to strictly uphold the 2–5 PM call window and to always give notice before any deviation.
fault_rationale: Jordan's lapse is taking a call outside the agreed window and not notifying Taylor; Taylor's lapse is holding a study group during the agreed quiet hours, both violating the same March 1 agreement.

title: Missing Turkey at Thanksgiving
background: Sarah and Mark are siblings who agreed to host a Thanksgiving dinner together. Sarah's home, Mark provides the turkey.
facts: On November 20, Mark and Sarah agreed that Sarah would host Thanksgiving dinner and Mark would bring the turkey.
Sarah sent a reminder to Mark on November 25.
Mark replied 'Got it, will bring the turkey.'
On Thanksgiving Day, Sarah prepared all other dishes and set the table.
At 3 PM, Mark arrived with a store-bought pie, but no turkey.
Sarah asked where the turkey was.
Mark said he forgot to order it, and the store was closed.
Sarah's other guests had to eat only side dishes for the main meal.
Mark offered to order pizza, but Sarah declined because they had planned a traditional turkey dinner.
Sarah later told her friend that she felt let down by Mark's lack of follow-through.
dispute: Mark wants Sarah to forgive him and not hold a grudge, and he offers to help with cleanup. Sarah wants Mark to acknowledge that he broke his explicit promise and to offer to host the next dinner to make up for it.
fault_rationale: Mark explicitly agreed to bring the turkey and failed to do so, while Sarah fulfilled her own responsibility by hosting and preparing all other dishes; Mark's excuse of forgetting is weak and not justified.

title: The RV Loan and the Kayak
background: Marcus and Elena are siblings. Elena borrowed $5,000 from Marcus to buy an RV for her family trips.
facts: On March 3, Elena asked Marcus for a $5,000 loan to buy an RV, promising repayment by December.
On March 5, Marcus transferred $5,000 to Elena's account without a written agreement.
On April 12, Marcus texted Elena: 'You need to send a payment schedule this week.'
On May 1, Elena paid Marcus $500, but did not send a schedule.
On June 15, Elena missed her June 1 payment and texted: 'Sorry, money's tight, we'll pay later.'
On June 20, Marcus saw social media photos of Elena's new kayak and camping gear.
On June 25, Marcus left Elena a voicemail saying he was 'disappointed' and that she was 'irresponsible.'
On July 2, Elena emailed Marcus explaining she used the loan for the RV, but had to spend $400 on new tires, offering only $100 that month.
On July 5, Marcus told Elena she had 60 days to pay the remaining $4,400 or he would take her to small claims court.
On July 10, Elena replied that she would stick to the original monthly plan and would not accelerate.
dispute: Marcus wants the remaining $4,400 paid in full within 60 days. Elena wants to continue with the original informal monthly payment plan.
fault_rationale: Marcus's lapses are the April 12 demanding text and the July 5 unilateral ultimatum, plus failing to set written terms; Elena's lapses are missing the June 1 payment, buying non-essential gear before paying the loan, and giving only a vague excuse without a concrete plan.

title: Scheduling Conflict in Elder Care
background: Karen and Tom are siblings caring for their elderly mother, who lives alone and needs help with shopping, cooking, and doctor visits. Karen lives nearby and handles daily needs. Tom lives three hours away and helps with finances and occasional visits. Their care arrangement has become strained over scheduling and decision-making.
facts: In January, Karen and Tom agreed that Karen would cover weekdays and Tom would arrange weekend respite care.
Tom did not book any weekend respite for March.
Karen posted the care schedule for March on the family calendar in February.
On March 12, Tom told Karen he had other plans for March 14-15.
Karen hired a temporary aide for March 14-15 and March 21-22 without telling Tom.
In April, Tom booked a sitter for April 18-19.
The sitter canceled on April 17 at 6 PM; Tom informed Karen on April 18 at 9 AM.
Karen called their mother on April 15 and mentioned Tom's missed weekends in March.
Tom sent Karen an email on April 20 saying she was "overstepping" and that he was not allowed to help.
From January to April, Tom contributed $200 per month toward care costs.
dispute: Karen wants Tom to commit to specific weekend dates or reimburse her for the hired aides she arranges when he doesn't. Tom wants a larger voice in care decisions and wants Karen to stop making unilateral moves like hiring aides and complaining to their mother.
fault_rationale: Karen's unilateral hiring and complaint to their mother are lapses; Tom's missed March booking and delayed cancellation notice are lapses.

title: The dented bumper
background: Marta lent her car to Leo for a weekend road trip, and it came back with a new dent on the rear bumper.
facts: Marta lent Leo her car for a weekend trip.
Leo returned the car two days later than agreed.
Marta found a dent on the rear bumper after the trip.
Leo said the dent was already there when he took the car.
Marta didn't photograph the car before lending it.
Leo didn't inspect the car before returning it.
Marta had told Leo about an unrelated scratch on the front bumper.
Leo returned the car with a half-empty fuel tank, despite promising a full tank.
Marta learned that the rear camera had been broken for weeks and hadn't mentioned it to Leo.
Leo sent a rude text to Marta after she demanded he pay for the dent.
dispute: Marta wants Leo to pay for the dent repair (estimated $350). Leo wants Marta to acknowledge the dent was pre-existing and stop blaming him, and he refuses to pay because of her lack of documentation.
fault_rationale: Marta's lapses: she failed to document the car's condition and didn't disclose the broken camera, undermining her claim; Leo's lapses: he returned the car late and with a half-empty tank, and sent a rude message, making him less trustworthy.

title: The Pocket Watch Inheritance
background: After their mother's death, Linda discovers that her brother Mark took the gold pocket watch that the will explicitly left to her.
facts: Mother's will dated March 15, 2023, names Linda as the recipient of the gold pocket watch.
The watch was stored in the family safe at mother's house.
On May 5, 2023, Mark visited mother's house and took the watch from the safe.
Mark did not inform Linda about taking the watch.
On May 12, 2023, Linda noticed the watch missing and asked Mark about it.
Mark admitted taking the watch but claimed mother promised it to him.
An email from mother to Linda on April 2, 2023, states she changed her will to give the watch to Linda.
Mark's only evidence is a vague memory of a 2019 conversation where mother said she might give him the watch if he cared for it.
Mark provides no written proof or witnesses for his claim.
Mark refuses to return the watch, insisting it is rightfully his.
dispute: Linda wants Mark to return the watch to the estate for proper distribution; Mark wants to keep the watch, citing a claimed verbal promise.
fault_rationale: Mark clearly violated the explicit will and took the watch without permission, while Linda acted reasonably by asking for its return; his weak excuse of a verbal promise lacks evidence.

title: Babysitting mix-up: Who is to blame for the canceled arrangement?
background: Maria and Elena have an informal arrangement for babysitting. Elena often helps out but sometimes has scheduling conflicts. They communicate via text.
facts: On March 1, Elena agreed to babysit Luca on March 15 from 6 pm to midnight.
Maria accepted this agreement and requested the evening off from work.
On March 10, Elena texted Maria that a work meeting might run late and she would update.
Maria did not reply to that text.
On March 12, Elena texted Maria that she confirmed she could arrive by 6 pm but needed to leave by 10 pm.
Maria did not reply to that text either.
On March 14, Maria booked a different babysitter for the evening and did not inform Elena.
On March 15 at 5:30 pm, Maria texted Elena: "No need to come, we made other plans."
At 6:10 pm, Elena arrived at Maria's house with a birthday cake for Luca.
Maria and Luca had already left with the other babysitter, and Elena waited outside until 6:50 pm.
dispute: Maria wants Elena to apologize for repeatedly changing the schedule and for showing up unannounced after being told not to come. Elena wants Maria to apologize for ignoring her messages and unilaterally canceling without confirming.
fault_rationale: Elena's lapses: she changed her commitment twice and failed to firmly confirm her availability; Maria's lapses: she ignored Elena's texts and ended the arrangement without a direct confirmation.

title: Wedding Guest List Blowup
background: Liam and Olivia are planning their wedding, aiming for a 130-guest reception, but the guest list has become a flashpoint between them.
facts: Olivia's parents contributed $15,000 to the wedding fund on March 3.
Liam's parents contributed $5,000 to the wedding fund on April 10.
On May 1, Olivia sent a group text to both sets of parents listing the proposed 120 guests, including 50 from her side and 40 from Liam's side.
On May 2, Liam's mother replied to that text: 'That list excludes my three cousins and their families – that's 12 people.'
On May 10, Liam added his mother's 12 cousins to the list and emailed the venue to increase the headcount.
On May 11, Olivia told Liam in person: 'You can't just change the list without asking me.'
On May 12, Liam's mother booked non-refundable flights for her 12 cousins based on Liam's May 10 email.

On May 15, Olivia sent an email to both sets of parents stating the final list would be capped at 130 and that she had cut Liam's mother's cousins to keep her own extended family who had already booked flights.
On May 20, Liam told Olivia he was considering eloping because the planning was toxic.
On May 25, Olivia told Liam she would hold the ceremony with just her parents if he did.
dispute: Liam wants to reinstate his mother's 12 cousins to the guest list. Olivia wants the list to stay at 130 and does not want to include them, citing her own family's previously booked travel.
fault_rationale: Liam's lapse was unilaterally adding guests without consulting Olivia; Olivia's lapse was unilaterally cutting those same guests and issuing a final edict, plus her threat to exclude Liam.

title: The Costa Rica Ledger
background: Lindsey and Mark planned a family trip to Costa Rica but disagree over who should pay for the flights after a hotel booking failed.
facts: On Feb 20, Mark promised Lindsey he would cover all transportation costs for the family trip.
On Mar 1, Lindsey booked non-refundable round-trip flights for herself and Mark, total $1400, using her own credit card.
On Mar 1, Mark authorized a $800 charge for the shared Airbnb rental.
On Mar 3, the Airbnb charge was declined due to insufficient funds in Mark's account.
Mark did not tell Lindsey about the declined Airbnb until Mar 15.
On Mar 16, Mark offered to pay Lindsey $700 as his share of the flights.
Lindsey rejected the $700 offer and demanded he pay the full $1400 plus $300 for her two days of unpaid leave.
Lindsey texted Mark on Mar 17: 'Great planning, Dad. Thanks for nothing.'
On Mar 18, Mark cancelled the Airbnb and booked a single room at a cheaper hotel for himself only.
dispute: Lindsey wants Mark to reimburse her fully for the $1400 flights and the $300 lost wages; Mark wants Lindsey to accept his $700 compromise and stop blaming him for his financial shortfall.
fault_rationale: Mark broke a promise, delayed telling Lindsey about the failed payment, and made a unilateral hotel choice; Lindsey booked flights without confirming his ability to pay, sent a rude message, and demanded an unrelated expense.
